To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Xestospongins are SERCA pump inhibitors that act at vertebrate synapses.
Xestosponging C (Xe-C) is a specific inhibitor of SERCA in the frog neuromyuscular junction.
Xestosponging C (Xe C) acts on SERCA at a synapse.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of Ca2+ homeostasis at the neuromuscular synapse, in particular the role of internal Ca2+ stores.

the study of the effects of XeC in the frog neuromucular junction, where the Ca(2+) stores are dependent upon inositol 3,4,5- triphosphate receptor (IP3R), and in the frog sartorius muscle, where the stores are ryanoidine receptor (RyR)-sensitive.
the identification of a novel class of SERCA pump inhibitor, XeC, that acts as a blocker of internal Ca2+ stores in the neuromuscular preparation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
XeC is a potent and selective inhibitor of the SERCA pump in the IP3-dependent Ca2+ stores of PSCs and the ryanodine-dependent Ca2+ store of motor terminals.

XeC is an inhibitor of the Ca2(+)-ATPase of the sarcoplasic/endoplasmic Ca2+ stores, which in the frog neuromuscuar junction, are IP3-sensitive in PSCs and ryanodine-dependent in motor nerve terminals.

XeC blocks the refilling of Ca2+ stores, but not the release, in PSCs and prolongs the recovery phase of the Ca2+-entry transient, but does not affect Ca2+ entry, in nerve terminals.
XeC is a specific inhibitor of SERCA in frog neuromusical junction.
XeC is a potent inhibitor (K(I)= 1.4 microM) of SERCA, but not of the Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaM kinase II).
The main takeaway from our work is that
SERCA inhibition by XeC has different effects on Ca2+ stores depending on their nature.
the effects of XeC are specific to the SERCA pump of the internal stores, and that the Ca2+ release mechanism is not involved in the effects of Xec.
XeC, a potent SERCA inhibitor, has no effect on the Ca2+ entry phase of Ca2+-dependent exocytosis at the vertebrate neuromuscular synapse.
